Surah al-Qiyamah (The Resurrection)

It is also called Surat La Uqsimu, and it is Meccan without any reported dispute or exception. There is a difference of opinion regarding its number of verses: according to the Kufan reckoning it has forty verses, and according to others thirty-nine. The disagreement concerns ﴿to hasten with it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16].

When the Exalted said at the end of al-Muddaththir, ﴿Nay, but they do not fear the Hereafter﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 53], after mentioning Paradise and Hell, and their not fearing them was due to their denial of the Resurrection, He, Majestic and Exalted, mentioned in this surah the proof for it in the most complete manner, described the Day of Resurrection, its terrors and its conditions, then mentioned what precedes it: the departure of the soul from the body, and then what precedes that: the beginning of creation, in the reverse of the actual sequence. So the Mighty One, the Great Speaker, said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾. The insertion of the negative particle lā before the verb of swearing is a common form, widespread in their speech and poetry. Imru' al-Qays said:

"No, by your father, daughter of al-'Amiri, the people do not claim that I flee."

And the saying of Ghawiyya ibn Salma, lamenting:

"Umama called out with a cry, so that she would grieve me. No, by you, I do not care."

The summary of what Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) held in this matter is that lā, when it occurs within speech, as in His saying, ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], is then a supplementary particle (ṣilah) added to emphasize the oath, like its occurrence in His saying, ﴿so that he should not know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], for emphasis of knowledge. And when it occurs at the beginning, as in this surah and in Surat al-Balad, it is for negation, because the supplementary particle occurs only in the middle of speech. Its rationale is that the formation of an oath implicitly contains information about the magnification of the thing sworn by. So it is a negation of that implicit statement, by way of metonymy (kinayah). The meaning is that it is not magnified by swearing, because it is in itself great; he swears by it first, and from this magnification he ascends to the emphasis of what is sworn to, since exaggeration in magnifying the thing sworn by implies exaggeration in the matter itself. As for what occurs to some minds, that it would follow that on this view it is information and not an act of swearing, and thus does not require an answer, and that the meaning rests on magnifying the thing sworn to rather than the thing sworn by, this is refuted.

Beyond this there are other opinions. It has been said that it is for negating the act of swearing, because the matter is clear. Al-Farra' said: it is for negating a statement known before the oath, and he refuted this. So they, here, denied the Resurrection, and it was said, "No," meaning: the matter is not so; then it was said, ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾. Al-Imam criticized this on the ground of repeating the negative particle after "wa" (and). It has also been said that it is not lā at all, but the lam has been lengthened in its vowel, so that an alif appeared from it, and the original is "la-uqsimu," as Qunbul recited, and it is reported from al-Bazzi and al-Hasan. According to some it is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), and the original is "la-anā uqsimu," with the subject omitted for it being known. The lam of emphasis entered upon the present-tense verb, as in ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them﴾ [al-Nahl: 124], and the original, according to some, is "innī la-uqsimu." And the lam of the oath did not take the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) with it, because that is not obligatory; it is rather the majority practice, as related from Sibawayh, while relying on the meaning according to others.

The majority said: it is a supplementary particle, and al-Zamakhshari chose this in al-Mufassal. What he mentioned of the restriction is not accepted, because if the addition is established in the oath, there is no difference between the beginning of speech and its middle; and the claim that the Qur'an is in the status of a single surah, connected part to part, is not accepted either, because its being so is in relation to contradiction and the like, not in relation to a ruling of this kind. Then he understood what he mentioned concerning the negative interpretation from the wording to be far-fetched, and the status of the remaining opinions is not hidden. Some of the discussion on this has already passed, so reflect upon it.

The discussion of His saying ﴿Nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾ follows that same pattern, except that earlier, regarding the reading *la-uqsimu* (I swear), it was said that the negation is intended here in the sense of "I do swear by the Day of Resurrection," because of its nobility, and "nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul," because of its baseness. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah what this implies, and it was related in *al-Bahr* from al-Hasan. Qatadah said: "This soul is the wicked, greedy one that blames its owner for what he has missed of the worldly pursuits and their aims." A similar report was transmitted from Ibn Abbas. The truth is that this is an interpretation that does not suit this context. For this reason it was said: it is the righteous soul that blames the souls on the Day of Resurrection for their shortcoming in piety, and the intensive form (*al-lawwamah*) is due to the abundance of the object of blame.

Mujahid said: "It is the soul that blames itself for what has passed, regretting evil for having done it, and regretting good for not having increased it. Thus it is always blaming, even if it strives hard in acts of obedience. The intensiveness lies in the manner, in terms of its continuity."

It was also said that the intended meaning of "the self-reproaching soul" is the genus of soul, encompassing both the pious and the wicked, based on what was narrated: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no soul, whether righteous or wicked, but that it will blame itself on the Day of Resurrection. If it did good, it will say, 'Why did I not increase it?' and if it did evil, it will say, 'Would that I had fallen short!'"

Its being joined to the Day of Resurrection is because the purpose of its establishment is its recompense and its raising on that Day. This was regarded as weak, since this degree of blame does not warrant being the object of an oath that exalts it, even if it proceeds from the believing soul that does wrong; how much less from the disbelieving soul which falls under the genus. It was answered that swearing by it in that case is without regard to the attribute, and the soul is considered in terms of its being noble, because it is the spirit, which is among the great matters of Allah, mighty and majestic. But it is objected that in that case mentioning the attribute yields no benefit.

The Imam (al-Razi) halted the report at Ibn Abbas and raised three objections to it, and he answered them by interpreting blame as wishing for more, and wishing that what occurred of disobedience had not occurred. What was mentioned about the justification for joining does not uniquely apply to this view, as is not hidden.

It was also said that the intended meaning is the soul of Adam (peace be upon him), for it has never ceased blaming itself for the act by which it was expelled from the Garden.

Most of the Sufis hold that the self-reproaching soul (*al-nafs al-lawwamah*) is above the commanding soul (*al-nafs al-ammarah*) and below the tranquil soul (*al-nafs al-mutma'innah*). They defined the commanding soul as that which inclines towards the bodily nature, commands bodily pleasures and desires, and draws the heart towards the lowly direction. They said it is the abode of evils and the source of blameworthy character traits.

They defined the self-reproaching soul as that which has been illuminated by the light of the heart to the extent that it has awakened from the slumber of heedlessness. So whenever an evil proceeds from it by virtue of its dark nature, it begins to blame itself and recoils from it.

They defined the tranquil soul as that which has been fully illuminated by the light of the heart, until it has divested itself of its blameworthy attributes, adorned itself with praiseworthy character traits, and become still from contending with the nature.

Some said that in ﴿al-lawwamah﴾ it is the tranquil soul that blames the commanding soul. Others said it is above the tranquil soul, being that which is prepared to educate others, and so on. The well-known view among them is to divide the stages of the soul into seven, of which these three are part. In *Sayr al-Suluk ila Malik al-Muluk* there is a valuable discussion on this, so whoever wishes may refer to it.

The answer to the oath is what is indicated by what precedes it.

The exegete's words, "Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?" Then: it is [the answer], "he will surely be raised." It was also said that it is "Does man think..." etc. And it was said.

"Yes, [We are] able" (﴿بَلى قادِرِينَ﴾). Both of these [views] are utterly baseless, like the claim that there is no need for a response (jawab), because what is intended is the negation of the oath. By "the human being" (al-insan) is meant the species (al-jins), and the hamza is for denying what occurs and deeming it abhorrent, and for rebuking him for it. And (inna) is the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafa min al-thaqila), its noun being a deleted pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), i.e., "Does man think that the matter is that We will not gather his bones after they have been scattered?" Its summary: why should this vain supposition, devoid of any indication and contrary to the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin) and its plain sense, occur? The attribution to the species is because among them are those who suppose this; indeed, perhaps most of them do. It is also permitted that the definite article be for a specific reference (al-'ahd), and that by "the human being" is meant 'Adi ibn Abi Rabi'a and the brother-in-law of al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, the two of whom the Prophet ﷺ used to say about: "O Allah, suffice me against the two bad neighbours." It is reported that he came to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and said: "O Muhammad, tell me about the Day of Resurrection: when will it be, and how will its affair be?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed him, and he said: "Even if I witnessed that day, I would not believe you, O Muhammad, nor have faith in it, unless Allah gathers these bones." Then this was revealed.

It was said [the person was] Abu Jahl, for it is reported that he used to say: "Does Muhammad claim that Allah will gather these bones after their decay and dispersal, and restore them as a new creation?" Then this was revealed. This is not like the intention of the species, and the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) does not restrict it. The mention of the bones indicates that the meaning concerns the restoration of the human being and the gathering of his scattered parts, since they are the mould of creation.

Qatada read "tujma'" with a upper dot (ta' fawqiyya) in the passive voice, with "'izamahu" in the nominative as deputy subject (al-niyaba). "Yes" (bala), i.e., We gather them after their dispersal and their return to being decayed remains and dust, in the depths of the seas and the vast deserts, wherever they may be, [while] We are "able" (qadirin). Here "qadirin" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the subject of the verb understood after "bala"; this is the view of Sibawayh. It was also said it is accusative as the predicate of kana, i.e., "Yes, We were able at the beginning; will We not be able in the restoration?" And he (the author) said: "This is, as you see, [weak]." It was said it is accusative because it occupies the position of "naqdiru" (We are able), since the estimate is "bala naqdiru," so when it was placed in the position of the verb it took the accusative. Makki related this and said it is far from correct, for it would necessitate the accusative of "qa'im" in your saying "marartu bi-rajulin qa'imin," since it occupies the position of "yaqum." So reflect.

Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn al-Sumaifi read "qadirun" (We are the ones who are able), ﴿عَلى أنْ نُسَوِّيَ بَنانَهُ﴾ ("to make even his fingertips"). "Banan" is a collective noun of kind whose singular is "banana," and al-Raghib explained it as "fingers." Then he said: it was said it was so named because through it arise the conditions by which a person can make clear what he wants, i.e., he sets others right with what is small among the bones of the extremities, such as the hands and feet. In the Qamus: "banan" is the fingers or their tips. So the meaning is: We gather the bones, being able to assemble them and restore them to their original structure, and to make even his fingers, which are his extremities and the last thing through which his creation is completed; or [the meaning is] to make even and join his phalanges, though small and fine, one to another as they were at first, without deficiency or disparity; how then with the large bones and what is not in the extremities? And in the stated circumstance, namely "qadirin 'ala" and so on, following the indication of restriction, there is an emphasis on the meaning of the verb, because gathering is among the acts that necessarily require power; so when it is restricted to complete power, it is emphasized. The first sense of the meaning indicates the depiction of the gathering and that there is no disparity between restoration and origination in including all the parts by which the body's substance or perfection was sustained; the second indicates the establishment of complete gathering, for if He is able to gather the finest and, customarily, the most remote from restoration, then to gather others is more capable. Perhaps this is the more suitable to the context.

From both of these is known the point of singling out the fingertips for mention. It was said the meaning is: "Yes, We gather them, while We are able to make even his fingers and toes, making them one uniform thing like the camel's sole and the donkey's hoof, not separating them, so that he cannot do with them anything of what he does with his separate fingers that have joints and fingertips, of the various kinds of work, grasping, releasing, and achieving what he needs. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak. Perhaps the meaning is: We gather them while We are able to level them at the time of gathering, so the statement conveys the earlier emphasis but from another angle: that He, glory be to Him, if He is able to restore him in a way that involves changing some parts, then to follow the first pattern in all of it is more capable. Abu Hayyan related this meaning from the majority, but restricted the leveling in it to its being in this world, and said: in the statement there is a warning. Then he followed this by saying it is contrary to the apparent meaning intended by the flow of the discourse. The matter is as he said: "If it were as he did, then do not be heedless."

It is not hidden that in the use of "la" at the beginning and the omission of the answer of the oath, and in the saying of Him, glory be to Him, "Does man suppose," and in observing the style of "wa-thana'ayka innaha ighrid" (by your front teeth, indeed they are...), there is an oath by the Day of Resurrection and what is resurrected in it. Then the preference for the word "hisban" (supposition), the use of the interrogative hamza of denial, attributing it to the species, and the particle of affirmation, and the circumstance following it, are among the exaggerations in establishing the desired matter, magnifying it, and condemning the one who turns away from preparing for it, things whose wonders dazzle. Then all beauty lies within the particle of transition (idrab) in His, glory be to Him, saying.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 75, verse 5:

﴿Nay, man desires to continue in wickedness before him.﴾ It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿Does he think...﴾ and is introduced for iḍrāb (a shift from one point to another, here from denying the supposition to informing about the state of the one who supposes) in order to convey something more blameworthy and reproachful than the first. It is as if it were said: "Leave off reproaching him, for he is more transgressive than that. And how could he refrain, when he desires to persist in his wickedness throughout the times before him and the time that lies ahead, and does not desist from it?"

Or it is conjoined to ﴿يَحْسَبُ﴾ (yaḥsabu), with the interrogative harmonized with it. Or it is conjoined to ﴿أيَحْسَبُ﴾ (a-yaḥsabu) with that meaning implicit in it, i.e., "Nay, I desire," introduced to add emphasis to the denial of this desire and to alert that it is more heinous than the first, to indicate that such supposing by itself is the desire for wickedness. This is like what we say in threatening a group who spread corruption in the land: "Do they suppose that the amir will not enter? Rather they desire to take possession of it." You would not say this except while escalating in denial, treating their frivolity as the desire to take possession and the disregard of the amir's standing. Jār Allāh (al-Zamakhshari) pointed to these two aspects, as he established in *al-Kashshaf*. The first aspect is more eloquent, because this is an escalation (tarāqqī), whereas the first is a turning away from denial and an implication that the matter is graver than that and graver still.

In both there is an indication that this person knows the gathering (of the dead) will occur, but he feigns heedlessness. The continuity was taken into account in ﴿لِيَفْجُرَ﴾ (li-yafjura, "that he may persist in wickedness"), because it is a report about the state of the wicked person: that he desires to persist in wickedness in the future. Moreover, his supposing and his desire are themselves the very wickedness.

It was also said that ﴿أمامَهُ﴾ (amāmahu, "before him") is a noun of place used figuratively here for future time, so it conveys continuity. Repeating the explicit noun a second time carries an evident threat and a censure of the foulness of what he has committed, and that human nature rejects this supposing and this desire. Returning the pronoun of ﴿أمامَهُ﴾ to this explicit noun is the most apparent reading.

From Ibn ʿAbbas there is a report that implies its pronoun returns to the Day of Resurrection, but the first is what the statements of many of the early generations (salaf) suggest. However, the first is apparent in the generality of wickedness. Mujahid, al-Hasan, ʿIkrima, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddi said regarding the verse: man only desires his lusts and his sins, so that he may proceed in them forever, charging ahead and obeying his hopes, and postponing his repentance. This is good and does not contradict that turning away. In it there is an indication that the object of ﴿يُرِيدُ﴾ (yurīdu, "desires") is omitted, and what indicates it is ﴿لِيَفْجُرَ﴾.

Some scholars said: it is treated as if it were the particle of intention (lām), and its verbal noun is implicitly governed by the lām of comprehensiveness, i.e., he directs all his desire ﴿li-yafjura﴾ toward wickedness.

From al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and those who followed them, regarding this type of construction: the verb is implicitly converted into a verbal noun in the nominative, governed by the inchoative (mubtadaʾ), and ﴿لِيَفْعَلَ﴾ (li-yafʿala, "in order that he do") is the predicate. Thus the estimate here is: "Nay, the man's desire is for the purpose that he commit wickedness."

﴿يَسْألُ﴾ a question of mockery, ﴿أيّانَ يَوْمُ القِيامَةِ﴾, meaning "when will the Day of Resurrection occur?" The clause is said to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it is also said to be an explanation (tafsīr) [of what precedes]. ﴿لِيَفْجُرَ﴾ [is in the same position], and it is also said to be a substitute (badal) for it.

The muḥaqqiqūn (the verifying scholars) chose that it is an explanatory resumptive clause (istiʾnāf bayānī), brought to give the reason for his determination to persist in wickedness, since it carries the sense of "because he denied the resurrection and mocked it." In this is [the point] that whoever denies the resurrection will inevitably commit the gravest wickedness, and [it contains] a portion of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿هَيْهاتَ هَيْهاتَ لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ ("Far, far is what you are promised") and ﴿إنْ هي إلا حَياتُنا الدُّنْيا﴾ ("There is nothing but our life of this world") [al-Muʾminūn: 36].

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 75, verses 7–9:**

﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾: it is bewildered and terrified. Its root is from *baraqa al-rajul* (the man was dazzled), when a man looks at lightning and his sight is stunned. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Even if Luqman the Wise were confronted, with his eyes, by Mayy unveiled, he would almost be dazzled.*

Its counterpart is *qamara al-rajul*, when a man looks at the moon and his sight is stunned. Likewise, *dahiba* (he was stunned) and *baqara* (he was bewildered) are used for being stunned by looking at gold and cattle. This is a *istiʿarah* (metaphor) or a *majaz mursal* (a sent or general metaphor, the figure in which a word is used for its concomitant or in its general sense).

Nafiʿ, Zayd ibn Thabit, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Aban (on the authority of ʿAsim), Harun, Mahbub (both on the authority of Abu ʿAmr), and other readers read *baraqa* with a fatḥah on the *rāʾ*. It is said that this is a dialectal variant of *bariqa* with a kasrah. It is also said that it derives from *al-bariq* (glittering), meaning it shone because of the intensity of its staring.

Abu al-Sammal read *balaqa* with a *lām* in place of the *rāʾ*, meaning it opened and was wide apart. It is said: *balaqa al-bab*, *ablaqtuhu*, and *balaqtuhu* (I opened it). This is the view of the lexicographers, except al-Farraʾ, who says *balaqahu* and *ablaqahu* mean he closed it. Thaʿlab rejected this, and some claimed that it is among the *al-adhdad* (words with opposite meanings). The apparent view is that the *lām* is original, but it is permissible that it is a substitute for the *rāʾ*, since the two interchange in some words, such as *natara* and *natala*, and *wajara* and *wajala*.

﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾: its light is gone. Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Zayd ibn ʿAli, and Yazid ibn Qatib read *khusifa al-qamaru* in the passive form.

﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾: where Allah brings them out from the west, as is related from Ibn Masʿud. The eclipse (*khusuf*) does not contradict this, since what is meant is not the technical term of the astronomers (*ahl al-hayʾah*), which is the going of the moon's light due to the opposition of the two luminaries and the earth coming between them. Rather, it is the going of its light due to a special manifestation on that day, or due to its conjunction with the sun, which is the *mihaq* (the dark phase of the moon).

It is permissible that the eclipse is meant in the technical sense, and that it is taken at the middle of the month for example, while the joining is taken at its end, since the sublime text gives no indication that their two times coincide. You know that this is an eclipse that disgraces the condition of the astronomers, and it hardly occurs to them, as does the aforementioned joining.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related, on the authority of ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasar, that he said: "They will be joined together and then hurled into the sea, and it will become the great fire of Allah." Widening the sea or making the two smaller is nothing that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cannot do. The conditions of the Day of Resurrection are contrary to the natural order, and its events are matters beyond nature. So one does not ask where the sea is in relation to the body of the moon, let alone the body of the sun, which in comparison to it is like a gnat compared to an elephant, nor how they are joined and hurled.

It is said: they will be joined as two black, rolled-up things, as if they were two bulls being slaughtered in the fire. It is related from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn ʿAbbas that they will be joined and placed in the light of the veils. It is also said that they will be joined and brought near to the people, so that sweat will overtake them because of the intense heat. And it is said that they are joined in the loss of light.

It is related from Mujahid, and it is the preference of al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj, that *al-jamʿ* (the joining) is a metaphor for equality in attribute. This view has a weakness, since if that were intended, the apparent wording would have been to say from the beginning: *khasafa al-shamsu wa al-qamaru* (the sun and the moon were eclipsed). There is no difficulty in attributing *khusuf* to both of them linguistically, and likewise *kusuf*. The verb did not take the feminine marker, due to its being placed before them and because the sun is feminine only metaphorically, and in such cases both options are permissible. The choice of omitting the marker was to observe the condition of the moon, which is coupled with it. Al-Kisaʾi said: the masculine form was used in consideration of the meaning, and the estimated sense is: "the two lights were joined" or "the two radiances were joined." But this is not the case.

﴿Man will say on that Day: "Where is the escape?"﴾ That is, on the day when these matters occur. ﴿Where is the escape?﴾ That is, the fleeing, in despair of it. It is also permitted to keep it as a genuine question, because of his bewilderment and confusion.

Al-Hasan (the grandson of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)), al-Hasan ibn Zayd, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, and a large group recited ﴿al-mafarr﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the fa, as an ism makan qiyasi (a noun of place formed by the regular pattern) from yafirru with a kasra, meaning: where is the place of fleeing? It is also permitted that it be a masdar (verbal noun), like al-marji'.

Like a boulder of rock that the torrent has rolled down from a height.

There is disagreement about this day. Most scholars hold that it is the Day of Resurrection, and this is the preferred view. ﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke against seeking refuge and wishing for it. ﴿La wazar﴾: there is no refuge (malja'). Its root meaning is the unassailable mountain. It was commonly a place of refuge for the Arabs when they fled, and it is derived from the word *wizr*, meaning burden. It then became common usage and came to refer literally to any refuge, whether a mountain, a fortress, a weapon, a man, or other things. From this is the verse of the poet:

*By your life, a young man has no refuge*
*From death that overtakes him, nor from old age.*

﴿Ila rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr﴾: that is, to Him alone, exalted is He, is the resting place of the servants. In other words, there is no refuge or escape for them except Him, mighty and majestic is He. Or, to His judgment, exalted is He, is the settling of their affair; none judges in it except Him, glorified is He. Or, to His will, exalted is He, is the place of their settling, whether Paradise or Hellfire. So whoever He wills, glorified is He, He admits to Paradise, and whoever He wills, He admits to the Fire.

The fronting of ﴿ila rabbika﴾ serves to indicate exclusivity (ikhtisas), even though its aspect varies according to the different meanings given to *mustaqarr*. As for ﴿Kalla la wazar﴾, it may be part of the speech of God Most High, said to the one who says ﴿Ayna al-mafarr﴾ on that Day, or it may be what is said on that Day, meaning to deter him from seeking flight and wishing for it on that Day. It may also be part of the speech of the human being himself, as if after saying ﴿Ayna al-mafarr﴾ he turns back upon himself, corrects himself, and says ﴿Kalla la wazar﴾. Whichever it is, the apparent meaning is that the words of God Most High ﴿Ila rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr﴾ are an *isti'naf* (resumptive new sentence), functioning as a justification for the sentence before it, or as a confirmation and disclosure of the reality of the situation. The address in it is to the master of those addressed, ﷺ. It is not proper for it to be among what the speaker is addressed with on that Day, nor among what he says to himself, because of the phrase ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day).

In *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*), it says: the apparent meaning is that the words of God Most High ﴿Kalla la wazar﴾ and ﴿Ila rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr﴾ are part of the speech of the human being. It has been said that it is the speech of God Most High, not a report about the human being, end of quote. There is discussion in this. It is also permitted that ﴿Kalla﴾ means *alla* (the introductory "indeed/verily"), or means *haqqan* (truly). So reflect, and do not be heedless.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 75, verse 14]**

﴿Nay, man is a witness against himself﴾. That is, a clear, manifest proof against himself, bearing witness to the evil deeds that proceeded from him, as the preposition *ʿala* (against) and the circumstantial clause after it indicate. *Al-insan* (man) is the *mubtada'* (subject of the nominal sentence), and *ʿala nafsihi* (against himself) is related to *basirah* (witness) by *taqdir i'mal* (the supposition that a word governs another word in the sentence). Alternatively, the meaning is *ʿalayhi* (against him) without any supposed governance. *Basirah* is a *basir* (one who sees, a seer) in form, and it is used figuratively (*majaz*) for a clear, manifest proof. Or it means *bayyinah* (clear), and it is an attribute of a supposed *hujjah* (proof), which is the *khabar* (predicate). The proof is described as "seeing" because its possessor is a seer of it, so the attribution is figurative (*majazi*). Or it means *dallah* (indicating) figuratively. It has also been permitted that there is an implicit and imaginative metaphor (*isti'arah makniyyah wa takhyiliyyah*) here. The feminine form is for emphasis (*mubalaghah*), or because the described noun, *hujjah*, is feminine. It has been said that the feminine form is used with the intention of the limbs, meaning his limbs are a witness against himself, that is, bearing witness. This is attributed to al-Qitbi. It has also been permitted that the supposition is *ʿayn basirah* (a seeing eye), and al-Farra' held this view and recited:

*As if upon the man of intellect there is a watchful eye,*
*in his assembly, or in a place where he is the one who looks.*

*He is wary, until he thinks all people,*
*out of fear, cannot fail to know his secrets.*

On this basis it has been said: *al-insan* is the first subject (*mubtada' awwal*), and *basirah*, with the supposition of *ʿayn basirah*, is the second subject (*mubtada' thani*), and *ʿala nafsihi* is the predicate of the second subject. The whole clause is the predicate of the first subject. Abu Hayyan preferred that *basirah* be the *fa'il* (agent) of the prepositional phrase, which is the predicate concerning man, and that it operates as an agent because it depends on that. The matter of the feminine form is clear. *Bal* (nay, rather) is for progression (*tarraqi*) on both views: the intention of a seeing proof and the intention of a seeing eye. The meaning, according to both, is ﴿man will be informed of his deeds﴾, *bal* (rather) there is in him what suffices instead of being informed, because he knows the details of his states and is a witness against himself by what he has done, since his limbs speak of that. ﴿On the day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [An-Nur: 24]. In both views, as it has been said, there is a trace of *tajrid* (abstraction, the figure of speech in which a speaker abstracts from himself a figure of the same kind), and it is more apparent in the second.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾: that is, even if he comes with every excuse by which he could defend himself. (The phrase) "hal" (circumstantial clause) is from the pronoun hidden in "basirah" or from the subject of "yunabba'u" (is informed). That is: he is a proof against himself, and he is a witness against it, even if he brings every excuse in defense of it. This contains an indication that defense has no currency for him. Or (the meaning is): he is informed of his deeds and will be recompensed and punished without doubt. Even if he brings every excuse, this is an emphasis on what is understood from the whole of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Man will be informed﴾, and so on.

The word "ma'adhir" is the plural of "ma'dhirah," meaning "excuse," contrary to analogy; the analogical form would be "ma'adhir" without a yā'. Al-Zamakhshari treated it as a collective noun (ism jam'), as is his habit in applying that label to plurals that go against analogy; otherwise it is not one of the patterns of collective nouns.

The author of al-Fara'id said: It may be said that the original form is "ma'adhir," and the yā' arose from lengthening the kasra, and this is, as you see, (weak). Or it is the plural of "mi'dhar" according to analogy, and it means "excuse." It has been objected that, in this sense, it has not been heard from reliable transmitters. Yes, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "al-ma'adhir" means "the curtains," in the dialect of Yemen, and its singular is "mi'dhar." This is also reported from al-Zajjaj. That is: even if he lets down his curtains. The meaning is that his concealment and hiding himself in this world will avail him nothing, because upon him is a witness from himself. There is in this an allusion to the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins testify against you﴾ [Fussilat: 22], and so on. It is also said that "basirah" upon him is the two recording angels, who write down whatever is good or evil. So the meaning is: nay, upon man are two recorders who write his deeds, even if he conceals himself with curtains. In the speech, according to this (view), there is no trace of tajrid (abstraction), as mentioned earlier. The use of "ilqa'" (casting) in the sense of "curtains" is clear. As for its use in the sense of "excuses," it has been said that the coming with an excuse was likened to casting a bucket into a well to draw water with it, so that what is intended by that is likened to water given to the thirsty. The saying of al-Suddi on this point indicates it: "even if he lowers (a bucket) with a proof and an excuse." It has also been said that the meaning is: even if he throws away his excuses, discards them, and surrenders. It has also been said: even if some of them shift (blame) onto others, as some of them say to others, ﴿Had it not been for you, we would have been believers﴾ [Saba': 31]. "Law" (even if) in all these views either has the conditional meaning stripped from it, as has been said, in which case it has no apodosis, or it retains its conditional meaning, in which case the apodosis is omitted and indicated by what precedes it. Al-Khafaji favored the first (view). In the verse, according to some of its aspects, there is evidence, as Ibn al-'Arabi said, for the acceptance of a person's confession against himself and the non-acceptance of his retraction from it. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

"So that you hasten with it" (﴿لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِ﴾) means: so that you take it in haste, for fear that it might slip away from you, according to what the words of the Scholar (al-Habr, i.e., Ibn 'Abbas) imply.

It has also been said that it is because of your excessive love for it and your eagerness to convey the message; this was narrated from al-Sha'bi. This does not contradict what was mentioned, and the preposition (al-ba') in both cases is for transitivity (al-ta'diyah).

Here, and likewise in what follows, "qur'anahu" is a verbal noun (masdar) like "ruj'an," in the sense of recitation, as in the words of the poet:

The meaning then is: "Indeed upon Us is its gathering," that is, its preservation during your lifetime, and its composition upon your tongue. It has also been said: "qur'anahu" is its composition and its collection, taking it as a verbal noun of qara'tu, meaning "I gathered." "When We have recited it," that is, when We have completed its recitation to you through the tongue of Jibril, peace be upon him, who conveys it from Us. It was also said: follow its recitation by study (al-dars), in the sense of "repeat it until it becomes firmly fixed in your mind."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verse 19:

﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation.﴾ That is, the explanation of what is unclear to you of its meanings and rulings, according to what has been said. It has been objected that it is possible for bayan here to mean disclosure (al-izhar), not the explanation of what is mujmal (general or ambiguous). It is authentically transmitted, through the narrations of al-Shaykhayn (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and a group of others, from the Habr (Ibn Abbas) that he said concerning this: "Then indeed upon Us is it to explain it with your tongue," and in another wording: "Upon Us is that you recite it." This is further supported by the fact that what is meant is the explanation of the entire Qur'an, while the mujmal is only part of it.

In that there is gradation and intensification in rebuke. Gradation would occur even if ﴿Do not move [your tongue]﴾ and so on had not been placed in between, but then the intensification of the rebuke would be lost. And [it follows that] if haste is not permissible in the Qur'an, which is healing and mercy, then how much less in that which is corruption and perdition? And the benefits mentioned above disappear. It is a digression (istitrad) which performs the function of an interjection (i'tiradh), and more eloquently. Some have called it an interjection (i'tiradh) without qualification.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Jahdari read ﴿yuhibbuna﴾ and ﴿yadharuna﴾ with the ya' of the third person in both, and the rule of connection for it is as has already been mentioned. As for the reading with the ta' [of address], it contains the prevalence of the addressee (taghlib al-mukhatab) and a shift (iltifat), which is the reverse of the first. This is the essence of what Jar Allah [al-Zamakhshari] alluded to, as has been reported.

They took that as evidence for what they claimed: that the Qur'an has been altered, substituted, added to and reduced. The scholars, the defenders of the Muslims and the shooting stars of the sky of religion, have refuted much of their speech with what has been mentioned above. The Imam [al-Razi] had views on it, some of which are good and some of which are not at all so. Al-Tibi said that His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Nay, rather you love the fleeting [life]﴾ is connected to His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾.

That is, it is said to the human being when he presents his excuses: "Nay, your excuses are not heard, for you have sinned and transgressed, and you thought that you would persist in your sinning, and that there would be no gathering, no reckoning, and no punishment; and that is from your love of the fleeting [life] and your turning away from the Hereafter." Here "faces" (wujūh) is the subject (mubtada'), "radiant" (nāḍirah) is its predicate (khabar), and "that Day" (yawma'idhin) is in the accusative, governed by "radiant." "Looking" (nāẓirah) in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿looking toward their Lord﴾ is a second predicate of the subject, or an attribute of "radiant," and "toward their Lord" is related to "looking." The indefinite noun (nakirah) was validly used as subject because the context is one of distinction (tafṣīl), as in the verse:

"So one day is for us, and one day is against us, one day we are made to suffer, and one day we are gladdened."

This is not because the indefinite noun became specified by "that Day," as Ibn ʿAṭiyyah claimed, since a time-adverb cannot be an attribute of bodies (judath), nor is it because "radiant" is an attribute of the faces and the predicate is "looking," as has been said, on account of the fact that it is generally the case that an attribute is known to the hearer as belonging to the thing described, whereas the faces' being capable of looking is not like that, so it should be stated as information. Indeed, many have mentioned this as a possibility regarding the verse, and Abū Ḥayyān said of it: "It is a permissible view."

The meaning of their being "looking toward their Lord" is that they see Him, may He be exalted, wholly absorbed in contemplating His beauty, to the extent that they become oblivious to anything else, and they witness Him, may He be exalted, in the manner that befits His essence, glorified is He. There is no restriction upon God, Mighty and Majestic, and to Him, exalted is He, belongs complete essential transcendence [p. 145] in all His manifestations.

And since exclusivity is established, taking it in that sense is invalid. The reply to this is that fronting does not purely signify exclusivity, especially since the requirement of maintaining the rhyme (fāṣilah) and emphasis is present. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verses 24–25:

﴿And faces that day will be scowling﴾: that is, extremely frowning. Bāsil is more intensive than bāsir, as has been said, but it has become predominant for the brave man whose fierceness is intense, so he turned away from it, because it gives the impression of a meaning that is not intended. By these faces he means the faces of the disbelievers. ﴿Thinking that a calamity that will break their backs will be inflicted upon them﴾: that is, a great calamity that breaks the spine, from faqara, meaning he struck his vertebrae. Abu 'Ubayda said: fāqira is from faqartu al-ba'ir, when I branded the camel's nose with fire. The subject of taẓunnu is a pronoun referring to the faces, with an elided noun: that is, their owners think. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers back to the faces themselves, taking wajh to mean the self (a device called istikhdam), but this is far-fetched.

Ẓann (supposition) has been said to mean certainty, and al-Ṭībī chose this view, arguing that the infinitive particle anna is not used after a verb of pure affirmation, but only after a verb of supposition or what conveys the sense of knowledge, so it can follow it, like the emphatic and light forms, as stated by al-Raḍī. It has also been said that it retains its well-known literal meaning, and that what is meant is that they expect this. Those who chose this view chose it, and there is no indication in it, through the contrast, that the seeing there has the meaning mentioned, as whoever claimed it claimed. The clarification of this is that what is done to them stands in contrast to looking upon the Lord, glory be to Him, since that is the utmost blessing, while this is the utmost retribution. The verb of supposition is used here to indicate that what they are in, though it is the utmost evil, may be followed by something worse, and so on forever. This is because fāqira here means a torment whose full extent cannot be grasped. So whatever is done to them of its severity, he infers from it another and expects something worse than it. When one is in supposition, it is harder upon him than if he knew it and had prepared himself for the matter. Moreover, knowledge concerns what is fixed and established, not what renews moment by moment. This is the reason for using the verb of supposition, and in the contrast he did not use a verb of supposition or knowledge, because those (the blessed) have reached what has nothing sought beyond it, and have tasted it. Then, after that, there is variation in that seeing in strength and weakness relative to the beholder, as he established. Perhaps this is an argument against the claimant, not for him. May God bestow upon us His favor through seeing Him.

﴿Kalla﴾ (No!). This is a rebuke against preferring the hasty life (al-'ajilah) over the Hereafter, as if it were said: "Desist from that, and take heed of what lies before you of death, at which the bond between you and the hasty life will be severed."

﴿Idha balaghat﴾ (When it reaches): that is, the soul (al-nafs) or the spirit (al-ruh), whichever is indicated by the context of the speech, as in the verse of Hatim:

*O Ma'wi, wealth does not avail a man*
*When the death-rattle comes upon him one day and his chest constricts.*

This is similar to the Arab saying "arsalat" (it sent forth), meaning "the rain came," and you will hardly hear them say "arsalat al-sama'" (the sky sent forth). Yet in this context the agent may be stated explicitly, so it is said: "balaghat al-nafsu" (the soul reached) ﴿al-taraqi﴾ (the collarbones), that is, the upper parts of the chest, which are the bones flanking the hollow of the throat on the right and left. It is the plural of taraqwah. They recited the verse of Duraid ibn al-Simmah:

*And many a great one has been lifted from them, while their souls had reached the collarbones.*

﴿Wa qila man raqin﴾ (And it is said: "Who is a healer?").

That is: those present around the dying person say, "Who will perform ruqyah for him and rescue him from what he is in?" Ruqyah is what is used to seek healing for one stung or ill, consisting of words prepared for that purpose, and among them are the verses of healing. Perhaps what is meant is the physician in general, whether he treats by word or by deed. What is apparent in this has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Abu Qilabah and Qatadah. According to some, the interrogation is genuine. It has also been said that it is an interrogation expressing dismay and denial, meaning: he has reached a stage where no one can heal him, as one says at the point of despair, "Who is able to heal this one who is near death?" This was related from 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd.

It has also been said that it is part of the speech of the angels of death, meaning: "Which of you will ascend with his spirit, the angels of mercy or the angels of punishment?" Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, paused on ﴿man﴾ and began with ﴿raqin﴾.

The majority read with idgham (assimilation). Abu 'Ali said: "I do not know what the reasoning behind his recitation is." Likewise he recited ﴿bal ran﴾ (al-Mutaffifin: 14). As for ﴿bal ran﴾, Sibawayh also mentioned in that case that clear pronunciation and assimilation of the lam with the ra' are both acceptable. He claimed that the literal meaning cannot be intended even if the soul were a body, because its reaching the collarbones is not realized except after its departure from the heart, and at that point death occurs; and one does not say ﴿man raqin﴾ as is apparent in the first view. Nor does what is mentioned afterward fit it, as you will know, God willing.

What the majority of the community holds, both earlier and later, is that the soul, which is the commanding spirit, is a very subtle body, finer than light according to those who hold it to be corporeal. The animal soul is its vehicle, and it permeates the body in the manner of the permeation of rosewater in the rose and of fire in charcoal, and of the flow of electric current according to those who hold it in bodies. The proofs for its corporeality are many, and Shaykh Ibn al-Qayyim has comprehensively set them out in his book *al-Ruh*, bringing wonders in it.

Some answered that this soul to which the reaching of the collarbones is attributed is the animal soul (al-nafs al-hayawaniyyah), not the commanding spirit (al-ruh al-amriyyah), which is a simple substance apart from the animal soul. Another answered that what is meant by its reaching the collarbones is the nearness of the cessation of attachment, and this is something that a simple substance can be characterized by, since it does not require motion, spatial occupation, or anything similar that is impossible for it.

He claimed that the literal meaning cannot be intended even if the soul were a body, because its reaching the collarbones is not realized except after its departure from the heart, and at that point death occurs; and one does not say ﴿man raqin﴾ as is apparent in the first view. Nor does what is mentioned afterward fit it, as you will know, God willing.

What the majority of the community holds, both earlier and later, is that the soul, which is the commanding spirit, is a very subtle body, finer than light according to those who hold it to be corporeal. The animal soul is its vehicle, and it permeates the body in the manner of the permeation of rosewater in the rose and of fire in charcoal, and of the flow of electric current according to those who hold it in bodies. The proofs for its corporeality are many, and Shaykh Ibn al-Qayyim has comprehensively set them out in his book *al-Ruh*, bringing wonders in it.

Then, the apparent meaning of reaching the collarbones is the approach of death and the nearness of the spirit's departure from the body. Whether you accept the necessity mentioned in the speech of that claimant or you do not accept it, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa qila man raqin﴾ (and it is said: "Who is a healer?") stands.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verses 28–29:

﴿And he will think that it is the parting.﴾ That is, the dying person will think that what has befallen him is the parting from his beloved, this world and its pleasures. It was also said: the parting of the soul from the body. The word "thought" (al-zann) here, according to Abu Hayyan, is in its own original sense, while most of the exegetes interpret it as certainty (al-yaqin). Al-Imam said: Perhaps certainty was called "thought" here because, as long as the person's soul is attached to his body, he hopes for life, out of his intense love for this hasty life, and his hope in it is never cut off. So certainty of death does not arise for him; rather, it is a dominant thought alongside the hope of life. Or perhaps he called it "thought" by way of mockery (tahakkum). ﴿And leg is entwined with leg﴾: that is, his leg is entwined with his leg and twisted around it at the panic and anguish of death.

This is as narrated from al-Sha'bi, Qatadah and Abu Malik. Al-Hasan and Ibn al-Musayyab said: they are the two legs of the dead person when he is wrapped in his shroud. It was also said that the meaning of their entwining is the ending of their matter and what is intended for them, meaning their death. It was also said: their drying up through death, and the lack of movement of one of them away from the other, so that they seem entwined. They are the first parts from which the soul departs, so they become cold before the rest of the limbs and dry up. Thus "al-saq" (the leg/shank) has its literal meaning, and the definite article in it is for a known reference (ahd) or a substitute for the genitive complement. Ibn Abbas, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid said so as well, and it is also a narration from al-Hasan. ﴿And leg is entwined with leg﴾ refers to the intensity of parting from this world due to the intensity of approaching the Hereafter, and the two become mixed. Similar to this is the saying of Ata': the intensity of separation from what is familiar: the homeland, family, children and friends, together with the intensity of coming before his Lord, exalted is His majesty, not knowing what He will do with him. So "al-saq" is an expression for severity, and it is a metaphor for that, and the definite article is for a known reference. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak: ﴿And leg is entwined with leg﴾: the drivers of those present with him, of mankind and the angels; these are preparing his body for the grave, and those are preparing his soul for the heaven. So it is as if their legs are entwined through the differing in going and returning and the repeated movements in affairs. This entwining is like the interlacing of spear points.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verse 30:

﴿To your Lord, on that Day, is the driving.﴾ That is: to Allah, the Exalted, and to His judgment is its driving, not to anyone else, on the basis that al-masaq is a mimi (ميمي) verbal noun, like al-maqal. The fronting of "ilaa rabbika" (إلى رَبِّكَ) serves restriction (lil-hasr). The statement involves an elided modifier (mudaf muqaddar), which is "judgment" (hukm). It has also been said that it is "promise" (maw'id), and what is meant by it is Paradise and Hell. It has also been said that there is no elided modifier, and that the Lord, majestic is His station, is the one who drives, i.e., the driving of these people is entrusted to your Lord and not to anyone else. The apparent meaning is what has preceded. Then, whether this is about the wicked person or about what encompasses him and the righteous, what is meant by "driving" is the driving that suits the one being driven. And this verse, by my life, is glad tidings for the one whose opinion of his Lord is good, and who knows that He is the Lord whose mercy has preceded His wrath:

They said, "Tomorrow we will come to the abodes of the sanctuary, and the caravan will alight in their place."

I said, "I have sins, so what is my recourse? In what manner shall I meet them?"

They said, "Is not pardon among their qualities, especially toward one whom they have hoped for?"

Then, the answer to "idha" (إذا) is elided, indicated by what has been mentioned: that is, "whatever was, was," or "the true reality of the matter is revealed to the person," or "the human finds what he did of good or evil."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verses 31–32:

﴿So he did not believe⁠ (fa-la saddaqa)﴾, that is, he did not affirm what it is obligatory to affirm from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the Messenger (ﷺ), and the Qur'an that was sent down to him. ﴿Nor did he pray (wa-la salla)﴾, that is, what was enjoined upon him. The meaning is: he did not affirm, and he did not pray. Here "la" (fa-la, wa-la) enters upon the past tense, as in the verse of the poet:

Should You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much,
and what servant of Yours is there who has not sinned?

The pronoun in both verbs refers to the human being mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Does man think⁠...﴾ (ayahsabu al-insanu). The clause is coordinated with His words, glorified is He, ﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ according to what al-Zamakhshari held. The meaning, based on what you have learned, that the question is one of mockery and disbelief, is that he regarded resurrection as far-fetched and denied it. So he brought neither the foundation of the religion, which is affirming what must be affirmed, nor its most important branch, which is prayer. Then He emphasized this by mentioning its opposite in His words, exalted is He: ﴿But he denied and turned away⁠﴾, negating the suspicion of silence or doubt. That is, along with that, he manifested denial and turned away from obedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verse 33:

﴿Then he went to his people, swaggering.﴾ *Yatabakhtaru* means strutting with pride in that. Whoever has done something like this should fear that the wrath of God, exalted is He, will descend upon him, so he should walk fearful and humble, not joyful and strutting. The word *thamma* (then) here indicates astonishment. *Yatamatta* is from *matt* (stretching), since the one who struts stretches his steps. Its original form is *yatamattat*, and the *ta'* was changed into a weak letter (*harf 'illa*, a vowel-letter such as alif, waw or ya') to avoid the repetition of similar letters, as they say *tazanna* from *zann* (thought), whose original form is *tazannana*. Alternatively, it is from *matā*, which is the back, since the one who struts twists his back in swaggering, and so it is weak (*mu'tall*) according to the original root.

In a hadith: "When my nation walks the *mutayṭā'* (a swaggering gait), and Persia and the Romans serve them, He will place their might among themselves and give their wicked power over their best."

Al-Ṭībī made the coordination of this clause, expressing astonishment, with the meaning of ﴿He asks when the Day of Resurrection will be﴾, and what he prepared for it was only what would bring about his ruin and destruction. He said that God's words ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾ and so on are an answer to the question, inserted between the conjunct and what it is conjoined to for the sake of intense concern. And God's words ﴿Do not move [your tongue with it]﴾ and so on are a digression on what you have heard. He took *ṣaddaqa*, from *taṣaddaq* (giving charity), to be what is reported from Qatadah. Others said it is from *taṣdīq* (believing), meaning: he neither believed nor did he give his wealth or purify it.

Abu Hayyan said: "What appears is that it negates charity and prayer from him and affirms denial for him, as in God's words ﴿They will say: We were not of those who prayed. Nor did we feed the needy. And we used to engage in vain talk with those who engaged in it. And we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43–46]. Taking it to negate belief requires that it be ﴿but he denied﴾ as a repetition, and it would have to be a *istidrāk* (corrective conjunction) after ﴿nor did he pray﴾, not after ﴿so he did not believe﴾, because the two are consistent." There is room for examination here, which is known from what we have established. Then he considered the coordination with God's words ﴿He asks﴾ and so on to be far-fetched, and he mentioned that the verse was revealed about Abu Jahl. He almost stated this explicitly in God's words ﴿yatamattā﴾, for that was his gait and the gait of his people, the Banu Makhzum, and he used to do it a great deal. He did not explain the status of the coordination on this basis. You know that the coordination does not preclude the narration that it was revealed about Abu Jahl. It has also been said that God's words ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ were also revealed about him. Passing judgments on a category does not harm the specification of some of its members in one of those judgments. Yes, there is no doubt that this coordination is distant in wording, but its distance in meaning is open to discussion, and perhaps what follows will strengthen the case for coordination with that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verses 34–35:

﴿Nearer to you [destruction], and nearer﴾. It is derived from *al-wali* (proximity), so it is in origin a comparative form (*tafdil*, the form expressing "more/most"), but it came to be used for nearness to ruin and for calling down evil. It is as if it were said: "Ruin is nearer to you," meaning: "May God destroy you with a destruction nearer to you than every evil and ruin." This is like how *bu'dan* (far away) and *suhqan* (away with you) became used for ruin. In *al-Sihah* (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), on the authority of al-Asma'i (*'an al-Asma'i*): "*qaraba-hu ma yuhlikuhu*," meaning that what would destroy him came near to him, that is, descended upon him. He recited:

*"So he (the enemy) was overtaken between two of its (the she-camel's) hind legs, and it was nearer that it should exceed three [strikes]."*

That is, it came near. Then he said: Tha'lab said: "No one has said anything about *awla* better than what al-Asma'i said."

On this view, *awla* is a verb with a hidden pronoun in it referring to the ruin, by the indication of the context, and the *lam* is extra, according to what has been said. It was also said that it is a past verb in the optative sense, from *al-wali* too, except that its subject is a pronoun for God Most High, and the *lam* is extra: "God has brought close to you what you dislike." Or the *lam* is not extra: "God has brought ruin near to you," which is close to what was reported from al-Asma'i.

On the authority of Abu 'Ali: ﴿Awla laka﴾ is a proper name for woe (*al-wayl*), built on the pattern *af'al* from the word *al-wayl*, by metathesis (*al-qalb*), and its original form is *awyal*. It is not declined (*ghayr munsarif*) because of being a proper name and the pattern. So it is a subject (*mubtada'*) and *laka* is its predicate. But there are objections: that *al-wayl* is not declined, and that like *yawm/aywam* (a rare form) even though it is not regularly formed, it is never used separately from the word it describes; that metathesis goes against the original form and is not to be assumed except with evidence; and that a generic proper name (*'alam al-jins*) is something outside analogy, and is hard to conceive especially in the present context. It was also said that it is an *ism al-fi'l* (a verbal noun used as a verb) built on fixed form, and its meaning is: "Woe to you, evil after evil."

A group chose that it is an *af'al al-tafdil* with the meaning "better" or "more fitting," and that the predicate of a deleted subject. The subject is supposed as fits the context, so the sense here is: "The Fire is more fitting for you," that is, you are more deserving of it and worthy of it. ﴿Then nearer﴾, ﴿then nearer to you, and nearer﴾ is repetition for emphasis, and the discussion of that has already passed, so recall it. Apparently the sentence is a concluding appendage to the invocation (*tadhyil li-l-du'a'*), with no place in terms of *i'rab* (grammatical case-analysis). It is also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with the verb "say" supposed, as if it were said: ﴿Then he went to his family, swaggering﴾, being told: ﴿Nearer to you…﴾, etc. This is supported by what al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim (who declared it sound) and 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported: "From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about God's words ﴿Nearer to you, and nearer﴾: Is it something the Messenger of God ﷺ said from himself, or did God command him to say it? He said: Rather he said it from his own self, then God sent it down."

He also used as evidence the words of the Exalted: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾, etc., that the disbelievers are addressed with the branch rulings (*furu'*). So do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verse 36:

﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾ I.e., left unattended, so that he is not held accountable and not recompensed. It is also said: that he is left in his grave and not resurrected. It is said: "Ibil sudan" (camels left to roam), meaning unattended camels grazing wherever they wish without a herdsman. "Asdaytu al-shay'" means "I neglected the thing," and "asdaytu hajati" means "I lost my need and did not attend to it." The poet said:

*So he swore by God with the utmost oath: God created nothing in vain.*

The accusative of *sudan* is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in *yutraka*. *An yutraka* occupies the position of the two objects of *yahsabu*. The interrogation is denunciatory (*inkari*). Its repetition after the words of Exalted God, ﴿Does man think We will not gather his bones?﴾ is to reinforce the denial of resurrection (*hashr*, the gathering of mankind for judgment). It was said that the speech, along with this, includes an indication of its occurrence, since wisdom requires commanding what is good and forbidding what is vile and base, and obligation is not realized except with requital, which may not take place in this world, so it must take place in the Hereafter. Some have made this a rational argument for the occurrence of resurrection, and there is a discussion in it that is not hidden.

Al-Alusi's commentary on verse 37 of surah 75:

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted (min manīy yumnā)?﴾ and so on, is a resumptive statement (istinaf) that comes to nullify the reckoning mentioned earlier. Its basis, since their objection was to resurrection (al-i'adah), was to repel that by means of the beginning of creation.

Al-Hasan read "alam taku" (ألمْ تَكُ) with the feminine second-person (tā' al-khitab), by way of iltifat (the shift from third person to second person). Most readers read "tumnā" (تُمْنى) with the upper tā', so the pronoun refers to the drop (nutfah), meaning: the man emits it (yumnīhā al-rajul) and pours it into the womb. On the reading with the yā', which is the reading of Hafs and Abu 'Amr, with a variant from him, and Ya'qub, Sallam, al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin, the pronoun refers to the semen (al-maniy).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 75, verses 38–39:**

﴿Then he was a clinging clot⁠﴾ meaning, by the power of God Most High, as God Most High said: ﴿Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. ﴿Then He shaped﴾ meaning, God the Mighty and Majestic decreed it, by making it, glorified is He, into a formed shape. ﴿And made﴾ meaning, He made it balanced and perfected. ﴿Of him He made⁠﴾ meaning, of the human being; it has also been said, of the semen, ﴿the two kinds, the male and the female⁠﴾ meaning, the two types. ﴿The male and the female⁠﴾ is an apposition (badal) to "the two kinds," and the hermaphrodite (khunthā) does not fall outside these two.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 75, verse 40:

﴿Is not That (the Great One of supreme majesty), who brought about this wondrous origination,﴾ ﴿able﴾, meaning capable, to ﴿give life to the dead﴾? And Zayd recited «yaqdiru» (يَقْدِرُ) in the imperfect form. It is easier than the initial creation by the measure of reason.

Talhah ibn Sulayman and al-Fayd ibn Ghazwan recited «ʿalā an yuḥyī» (عَلى أنْ يُحْيِي) with a sukun (vowel-less) on the yā'. You know that its vowel is an i'rab (grammatical inflection, the case-ending vowel), which is dropped only in pausal position (waqf). It has been found in poetry to be dropped without pause. It is also reported from some of them that «yuḥyiya» (يُحْيِيَ) was recited by transferring the vowel of the yā' to the ḥā' and assimilating the yā' into the following yā'. Ibn Khalawayh said: The people of Basra, Sibawayh and his companions, did not permit the assimilation in «yuḥyī», saying that the second yā' is sukun, and they do not count the fatḥah on it, because it is an inflectional vowel that is not obligatory. Al-Farra' permitted it and argued with the line of verse, «tamshī bi-shiddatin fa-taʿī» (تَمْشِي بِشِدَّةٍ فَتَعِي), meaning «fa-taʿiyā» (فَتَعِيا). In sum, the recitation is shādhdh (irregular, a non-canonical reading).

Several reports state that when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, he would say: «Subḥānaka Allāhumma wa-balā» (سُبْحانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وبَلى, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and yes"). In some of them: «Subḥānaka fa-balā» (سُبْحانَكَ فَبَلى, "Glory be to You, and yes").

Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim (who graded it sound) related from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you recites Surat al-Tin (the Fig) and reaches its end, ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾, let him say: «Balā, wa-anā ʿalā dhālikum min al-shāhidīn» (بَلى وأنا عَلى ذَلِكم مِنَ الشّاهِدِينَ, "Yes, and I am among the witnesses to that"). Whoever recites Surat al-Qiyamah (La uqsimu bi-yawm al-qiyamah) and reaches ﴿Is not That able to give life to the dead?﴾, let him say: «Balā». Whoever recites Surat al-Mursalat and reaches ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾, let him say: «Āmannā bi-Llāh» (آمَنّا بِاللَّهِ, "We believe in Allah")."
